en: The Sadhana of Guhyavajravilāsinī, the Essence of All Yoginīs, by the Siddhācārya Śrī Śabarapāda.
The Sadhana of Guhyavajravilāsinī.
The Essence of All Yoginīs. Om, homage to the illustrious Vajravilāsinī! In whom the multitudes of gods, asuras, lords of the gods, and lords of men [take refuge]...

I go for refuge to the feet of Śrī Lokanātha, those lotus-feet upon which bees fall with their heads, and which are the great treasure-trove of the ocean that accomplishes all spiritual attainments (siddhis). ||1||

She who is the Goddess Vajravilāsinī, the very Splendor, through her devotion to the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), spreads a wondrous and great festival of eternal bliss; she is like a yellow garment dyed with nirvāṇa, the suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient beings personified, and exceedingly radiant with passion.
I bow to her pair of feet, which cause the birth of the world and are most worthy of worship. ||2||
Nothing has been heard or read by this lowly mountain-dweller;
how many syllables could he possibly utter by virtue of his lordship over the world? (3)
In that delightful mountain, which consists entirely of jewels, is fragrant with the scent of musk deer, and serves as a place for the mind’s repose, he gave a foothold to the god of love. (4)
In that region, which was most delightful, filled with fragrant flowers, and resounded with the gentle warbling of cuckoos in its shimmering caves and mango groves; (5)
In the dense garden of red Aśoka trees, on the eighth day of the month of Aśoka,
this playful woman was taught by my preceptor, whose mark is compassion.
Through conduct in accordance with the rules and with one-pointed concentration of mind,
she was brought face-to-face by me while dwelling together with Śabarī.
Subjugation, attraction, immobilization, killing, and eradication;
as well as collyrium, pills, the sword-rite, and many other such [practices]. (8)
"Having obtained the state of Mahāmudrā, I have made this request with my speech:
to whoever shall meditate upon you according to the ritual procedure, you shall grant that fruit. (9)
One who has obtained the signs should write down, in brief, the essence of that means for awakening (bodhisādhana), the practice as it was taught by the Blessed One.

The supreme sādhana should not be given to those who are characterized by greed, nor especially to non-Buddhists who are joined with pride, nor to those of cruel mind who engage in acts of violence. (11)
The supreme sādhana should not be given to those beings who follow the Buddha or non-Buddhist paths, whose minds are not yet ripened, or who are distracted by divine visions and madness. 12.
This supreme sādhana should not be given to those who are lame, humpbacked, or afflicted by diseases of the throat; nor to eunuchs, nor to men and women whose minds are tormented by illness. (13)
The divine practice should be bestowed upon one who has received initiation and is purified, who possesses great knowledge, who is compassionate, and who is peaceful, beautiful, and grateful. 14.
The divine practice should be bestowed upon one who is satisfied by the service of the guru, who guards the secret confidence, and whose mind is intent on uplifting the lowly. (15)
This divine means of accomplishment should be bestowed upon men and women who are devoted to the welfare and benefit of sentient beings and who long for compassion and awakening. 16.

Having first understood the procedure for accomplishment after performing the propitiation of the guru, and being satisfied by the nectar of the guru’s words, one should then begin the practice. ||17||
In the midst of secret places such as mountain caves, which are the abode of fragrant flowers, Guhyavajravilāsinī should be meditated upon together with her consort. (18)
In an empty house, in one's own garden, or in a secluded forest, the Goddess should always be worshipped and practiced according to the prescribed rite. (19)
First, one should perform anointment with fragrant flowers and the like,
and wash the secret vajra according to the specific mantras and vidyās.
One should apply collyrium to the eyes and arrange the hair beautifully;
this should be done with the Vidyā for the sake of one's own radiance. (21)
One should form the palms like a lotus with many pairs of fingers;
it is soft to the touch and always fragrant, serving as a cause for happiness and good fortune. (22)
Her lower lip is as lovely as coral, her forehead adorned with vermilion,
a streak of lac upon her brow, and her ear decorated with an *aśoka* flower.
Having cast aside other ornaments, she wears a long necklace of pearls;
the practitioner likewise assumes the excellent form of Padmanarteśvara.
Having drawn forth passion together with knowledge, one should perform only that much [of the ritual] so that the mind does not become distracted. (25)
On each of the two fourteenth days and likewise on the eighth day, according to the prescribed rule,
one should worship the Goddess at night alone during four specific times within the month.
One should light a lamp there, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, so that the entire universe, as well as the image in its every limb, is especially illuminated. ||27||
Then, having sat down for the sake of accomplishment with a mind intent on the welfare of sentient beings, he, being composed in all Buddhas, set out to attain the state of Mahāmudrā. ||28||
Having abandoned shame and the like, as well as anger, greed, and so forth, one should utterly avoid even the slightest trace of disgust or hesitation. (29)
Seated comfortably in an even posture, naked and with hair disheveled, he should slightly contract his own right leg and extend the toes of the left foot. (30)
One should visualize the Vidyā situated between those two, clothed, with her hair loose, endowed with such beauty, and well-acquainted [with him]. (31)
Having applied a tilaka of Madhuka flowers to her forehead and abandoned the lotus-utkaṭāsana posture, one should move one's two arms like the two arms of the Goddess. 32.
Having fashioned a circular maṇḍala within her dharmodaya with saffron and red sandalwood using the finger of the nectar-hand of the left hand, ||33||
Thereafter, one should perform the mandala in that very place in the form of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya).
This mantra of the mandala has been taught in the Mantrodghāra. ||34||
Having recited this mantra, one should utter the sound "sīt.
With the first syllable of the mantra, one should offer a flower upon the navel.
The yogi should meditate on emptiness while abiding in the four divine abodes;
thereafter, he should mentally recite the mantra beginning with "Oṃ śūnyatā. (36)
One should place the five-syllable mantra of the Goddess in five locations:
on the head, the face, and the heart; and at the navel and the *vajra*, following the threefold sequence. (37)
Just as one has projected oneself upon the five locations of the Vidyā, so should one perform the worship of the mantra, setting aside the mantra of emptiness and the like. (38)
Then one should meditate upon the solar disc, which is the great passion of the rising sun—vast, most beautiful, red in appearance, and brilliantly blazing. (39)
There, having meditated upon the source of phenomena (dharmodayā) arising from the syllable *rakta* and others—
yellow, gladdening the mind, and radiant with flowing liquid lac— (40).
A stream of all sensual pleasures, shimmering with the play of suns and lotuses, characterized by all the modes of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body. ||41||
Through dramatic gestures and other means, one should perceive the world—red, mixed with the moon and sun, situated within the womb of the Bhaga—as revolving like a wheel. 42.
Above that is the great seed-syllable, having the form of molten gold,
the great five-syllabled mantra, blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon.
One should contemplate the extraordinary image as red, emitting garlands of fire that terrify the three worlds and pervade the Akaniṣṭha realm. 44.
The entire world, having become liquefied, should be seen as entering that mandala; the whole universe is brought under control for those beings whose minds are composed. 45.
The Goddess, transformed into this form, possessed the luster of the bandhūka flower; she was fair-complexioned, radiant like molten red gold, and adorned with her own innate beauty. 46.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with an *aśoka* flower on her ear,
bearing a line of red lac upon her forehead, and draped with a string of pearls.
Complete with all the auspicious marks, yet devoid of other ornaments;
possessing the desired beauty, she was naked and her earrings were removed. (48)
She stands upon a lotus raised high on a banner in the Lotus-Dancer posture, performing a dance in the utkaṭāsana position, her face curved with side-glances and smiles. ||49||
With her arms bent and raised, she brandishes a thunderbolt and a chisel;
in her left hand she holds a noose with its essence, while her girdle sways in playful motion.
Through the delights of embracing, she is the very essence of Padmanarteśvara;
with her shimmering touch, she possesses the grace of a dripping lotus.
She possessed the splendor of a shimmering expanse, throbbing with the sound of the clapping of her hips and loins;
through the process of quivering and contracting, she was as wondrous as the submarine fire (vaḍavā).
One should meditate upon that very Vajravilāsinī, the Vidyā standing before one, who colors the three worlds with a mass of nets of red rays. 53.
The seed-syllable Padmanarteśvara, possessing the power of the pollen-dust of the lotus, is the sprout of bliss from an equal seed that has arisen all at once. (54)
With the tips of his body hairs clearly manifest, his mind naturally attached [to her], endowed with all the auspicious marks, and possessing a form of sixteen years; ||55||
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with an *aśoka* flower on his ear, marked with a golden tilaka, and draped with a string of pearls. (56)
Endowed with her own natural beauty, devoid of other ornaments, a vessel for the essence of great passion, with disheveled hair and clad in the directions as her garment. (57)
O Teacher of Love, he lies somewhat supine upon his right leg, which is slightly extended while the left leg is drawn up and bent. (58)
With his two arms, he should perform a devout embrace with his breasts;
clearly manifesting his secret vajra, he causes the playful woman to dance. (59)
Holding a yellow lotus in his left hand and a vajra in his right, he embraces and repeatedly kisses [her] with constant playful grace. (60)
Performing the coitus with intense passion and uttering the neighing of a stallion,
his eyes were half-open from the savoring of the bliss of innate joy.
In this manner, one should meditate upon oneself as the Lord of Passion (Surateśvara), the all-pervading Padmanarteśvara, who is like great bliss and unmanifest. 62.
Therefore, by the rays of this Great Goddess, which are like molten gold,
the three worlds have become mutually unified and have become a vast ocean of nectar.
In the midst of that, one should perceive oneself situated together with the Goddess,
sporting and having attained the bliss of great passion, pervading the interior of the three worlds.
Immediately thereafter, one should quickly contemplate: "The Tathāgatas, the world-protectors, the kinnaras, asuras, and humans are consecrating me here before them. (65)
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and various hosts of Apsarases [honored him] with flowers,
incense, and other offerings, with musical instruments, and with great festivals of diverse dances.
Then, having entered the triple [mandala], one should perform the mandala worship;
by means of the worship of body, speech, and mind, one should purify the threefold action. ||67||
Having recited the root mantra, one should utter the name of the Goddess;
having performed the utterance "saḥ," one should worship the secret maṇḍala.
Having held flowers, fruits, and so forth with the left hand and the *vṛddhā* and *amṛta* [mudrās], everything should be offered with equal flavor, three times, without agitation. (69)
Having likewise worshipped one's own body as the vajra according to the graceful ritual, one should worship the mantra of the Goddess by means of the recitation of that very mantra. (70)
The forehead, the eyes, the throat, the nose, the two sides of the neck, the lips, the throat, the heart, the breasts, and the armpits—the wise one [should touch these]. (71)
Having worshipped the navel-pada, one should likewise offer the body [of the deity];
and there, one should offer fragrant incense according to the prescribed rite.
And for the Bhagavatī and Padmanarteśvara, the worship of the Vajrapīṭha and so forth should be performed at the beginning by that very same method of sequential yoga. (73)
Betel-leaf, well-filled with camphor and other ingredients, should be offered;
having partaken of it together, one should then recite the verses. (74)
O Narteśvara, you who are devoted to great bliss, you are non-different from me; grant me an embrace for our dalliance—salutations be unto you! 75.
O you who are devoted to great bliss, you are inseparable from me;
grant me an embrace for our dalliance, O playful one—homage be to you! (76)
Having recited this verse, one should perform mutual salutations with the gesture of joined palms (sampuṭāñjali) and with speech of sweet syllables. (77)
The world arises from a single seed and consists of wisdom and means;
the Goddess consists of all women, and the Lord consists of all means. (78)
O Great King, you are non-dual and intent upon the meaning of the innate (*sahaja*);
come, O one of great supernatural power through the vajra-mudrā, to perform the union (*melāpaka*). (79)
Having recited the two verses while first recollecting the mind, one should perform mutual embracing through the application of the "new flower" (navapuṣpī). ||80||
Embracing, kissing, the gentle massaging of the breasts, gazing, touching the vulva, causing it to expand, and the friction of the linga. ||81||
The elevation of the entry into the lotus occurs through three parts; it is proclaimed as being from the base up to the middle of the jewel in the nine-petalled [lotus]. (82)
A kiss should be given where [the deity] has been well-worshipped with flowers;
it extends from the head down to the feet, covering twenty parts of the body. ||83||
One should not inflict nail-marks for the sake of avoiding remorse;
rather, one should delight the form of the Goddess with the touch of fingernails and gentle scratching. (84)
The mouth-nectar should be drunk preceded by the neighing of a stallion;
likewise, the bite should be applied slowly by means of the striking down of a female dog's teeth. (85)
Having become somewhat relaxed, one should remain in the *devamudrā*;
the goddess dances with her own mudrā at the tip of the *bhidura*. //86//
From the immovable state, one should understand that happiness arises;
yet the mind is fickle due to agitation.
For one whose mind is attached to the innate goddess through effortless play, [the mind becomes steady]. (87)
What excellent boat has appeared to cross the waters of the ocean of passion?
Having obtained the arising of the Guru’s word, one should propel it with the sounds of the vehicle. 88.
Having recognized the three locations— the taking up, the releasing, and the coming and going of the vital points—
at the end of one's own movement, this life-force should swallow the unchanging void.
The place of churning should be understood as that which arises at the moment of the extraordinary [union];
one should agitate the Goddess with the vajra, yet not emit the bodhicitta. 90.
But when the thought of awakening has been relinquished, how can there be great bliss therein?
One should churn [the mind] with the desire for the innate nectar from the ocean of the lotus. (91)
And the kālakūṭa poison of dispassion does not arise, as one proceeds according to the previously described cultivation preceded by the goddess of the gods, whose essence is the nectar-ray. 92.
The wise one should cultivate that meditation which brings about the three worlds;
by means of the union of the churner and the churning, some kind of sphere (golaka) emerges. 93.
One should perform the sprinkling with that [liquid], preceded by the utterance of the seed-syllable;
one should cast the lotus-ball into whichever substances, such as wine, are present. 94.
By the mere act of satisfying that [the fire], the God and Goddess become well-pleased;
having slightly contracted with the hand the thunderbolt situated in the center of the lotus. (95)
The practitioner of mantra should slowly wave the two wings of the lotus, held stiffly with the thumbs and fingers of both hands; thus, the satisfaction of the Goddess arises. (96)
One should cause that which was joined to be opened, and likewise cause that which is expanding to remain as it is;
one should produce the joy of swaying and contract the lotus. 97.

With certain graceful movements of dance, accompanied by sidelong glances, smiles, and hand gestures, he [is situated] within a mandala pervading the three worlds with masses of light from his two arms. 98.
One should contemplate one's own form as playing with a playful woman, appearing like a city of Gandharvas and as flickering as the water of a mirage. 99.
The wise one should always practice the cultivation of the thought "so it is";
however, when weary from such cultivation, the yogi should perform recitation with his left hand. 100.
The five-syllable great seed-mantra, saluted by all the Buddhas, destroys the great sins accumulated over seven lifetimes. (101)
One should first cause the mantra, which rests upon the goddess’s lotus, is blazing, and resembles a red bee,
to enter from afar into one's own navel and then emerge through the nostril.
Having entered the nostril-passage of the Goddess by way of the lotus-path, one should behold it returned again to the vajra, having come and gone. 103.
They say this is "swinging recitation" (dolājāpa), because it brings about swift accomplishment;
one who is devoid of this supreme yoga does not achieve success through mere mudrā.
Having once uttered this together with the Vidyā in a beautiful tone—transcending sound, the point, and dissolution—this is the characteristic of recitation (jāpa). ||105||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the mutual adorning of the vajra and the lotus there, repeatedly with the Garuḍa-mudrā. (106)
With a joyful heart, one should offer the tenfold oscillation to the deities;
then, by that same yoga, the wise person begins the recitation (japa). ||107||
In this very sequence, this recitation should be performed according to the rules by the practitioner at that time, up to five hundred repetitions. (108)
At the conclusion of this recitation, however, one should contemplate the union with the Self (ātma-melaka), having entered the ocean of awakening for the sake of the supreme fruit. 109.
The world, arising from the great passion of the union (yuganaddha) and endowed with wisdom, takes the form of molten liquid gold, radiant with the state of equal flavor (samarasa). 110.
Whirling in a clockwise direction like a wheel,
it awakens the world from its afflictions, encompassing even the entire mandala of the three realms.

Even the wind of worldly passion attains peace when it is consumed by even a particle of ash from that which has been burnt down to its very root—the latent impressions nourished by the entire range of sense objects. (112)

Just as [the rainbow] vanishes into the ocean of the sky by way of Indra’s bow, that [sky] dissolves into the innate [nature], and the sky dissolves into the ocean of awakening, which is the great arising. 113.
Through the repeated practice of the latent tendencies of ignorance, ignorance itself is abandoned;
therefore, phenomena born of dependent origination are like the great dream that has arisen. 114.
Arising, abiding, and destruction indeed arise from conceptual construction;
since at the outset there is no such construction, awakening shines forth. (115)
Existence and non-existence are dissolved into their own nature.
Through the realization of the ultimate truth and so forth, there is nothing superior to suchness, which is free from both the real and the unreal. 116.
Thus, established in meditative absorption and rendered immovable by correct practice, the yogi then becomes perfected, possessing the great supernatural power of Mahāmudrā. ||117||
When the thunderbolt has arisen from knowledge, the mandala and other rites should be performed upon the seat;
the deity born from the Vajra-seat is the Self, and the playful consort is one's own self. (118)
And for those two, as before, everything such as meditation and recitation should be performed according to the prescribed rule, having attained the yoga exactly as described. ||119||
Then, as for how one should sport with a mind released from meditative absorption:
having himself meditated upon Narteśvara and the playful goddess by means of the Vidyā, [he should proceed]. (120)
The practitioner of mantras should worship daily during the fourth watch of the night;
according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
The existence of the Vidyā is in every way within one's own Vajrapīṭha;
having constructed the maṇḍala as before, one should perform the ritual for the daily worship.

The mudrā is also as before; the practitioner of mantra, meditating on the festival of passion with such a goddess—the entire [mandala] beginning with the sun, the dharmodayā, and so forth—[should perform] the union. (123)
Holding the vajra with the hand, one should caress it through the yoga of the great maṇḍala;
likewise, one should perform the recitation of mantras and so forth, and must not emit the bodhicitta. 124.
One should meditate on the union of means (upāyamelaka) within the maṇḍala of one’s own lotus;
having constructed the maṇḍala as before, one should perform the rite of daily worship.
Having joined the index finger and the thumb together as a well-united pair,
one should perform the recitation, meditation, and other rites by means of that vajra-lotus application.
Then the Master of Passion [should perform] the fourfold birth, the four arms, the divine fourfold oscillation, and the distinction of the four mudrās. ||127||
Indeed, just as one would hide a moving object from a thief, I have not written down the seed-mantra here in its explicit syllables and words. (128)
This [syllable] ending in *ā* has *lī* as its head; it flows forth with *jhā* at its end, followed by *rī*, *ru*, and *va* after *lī*. (129)

This five-syllable mantra, adorned with the moon-drop (bindu)—namely *e*, *ā*, *rī*, *ra*, and *brī*—is the bestower of the fruits of all desires; it should be recited according to the prescribed ritual. 130.
The power of the King of Mantras will become manifest;
for he is indeed exceedingly compassionate toward the great cow of all accomplishments. (131)

Rate surate nityaklinne madadrave sukhena sukhayone subale vihvale liṅgavajraṃ grasa grasa ha ha ha a a a mama sarvasattvānāṃ sarvasiddhiṃ dehi dehi saḥ ||132|| O you who are in union, eternally moist, flowing with passion, the source of bliss, the womb of happiness, the powerful one, the agitated one: swallow, swallow the vajra-linga! Ha ha ha! A a a! Grant, grant all accomplishments to me and to all sentient beings! Saḥ! ||132||
Then, having uttered the first syllable, one should utter the end of *surata*;
taking the second syllable, one should utter the end of *drava*. (133)
Having uttered the third syllable, it is well-recited ending with *sukhayoni*;
having taken the fourth syllable, it is chanted ending with *vihvalā*;
and having pronounced the fifth, one should recite *liṅgavajra* and so forth. (134)

Rāte surate! O you who are eternally moist and flowing with passion, VĪṂ! O you who bring happiness through happiness, RĪ! O powerful one, O agitated one, RA! [Seize] the vajra of the linga, BRĪ! Swallow, swallow! HA HA HA! A A A! Grant, grant all accomplishments (siddhi) for me and for all sentient beings! SAḤ! ||135||
This mantra is also recited during the offering of oblations (*validāna*).
A rosary (*mālā*) without [excessive] rays is excellent when well-dyed with madder (*mañjiṣṭhā*) and other dyes;
likewise, it may be strung with coral beads or *putrajīva* seeds. (136)
Or, having fashioned a beloved [image] from the fruits of the red sandalwood tree, one should construct a rosary according to the prescribed ritual, consisting of one hundred and eight beads. (137)
This noble conduct of the preeminent practitioner of yoga, as well as that of women, should always be observed; it is to be known as established in the ritual for attaining perfection. ||138||
One should not doubt one's own state, nor should the divine characteristic be performed; this is to be known in the rite for all accomplishments, exactly as taught by the Omniscient One. 139.
Within a month, or within six months, there shall be the attainment of breath and the desired fruit;
within a year, there shall be prosperity and supernatural powers (siddhi), preceded by the powers of subjugation and attraction. 140.
Having become servants, all beings—including gods, asuras, and humans—serve [him]; what then can be said of mortals such as Urvaśī and others? (141)
For those who are constantly devoted to practice, when twelve years have been properly completed, the practitioner becomes a Siddha, having ascended to the state of Mahāmudrā. ||142||
Having recollected what was previously taught, one should practice that immediately thereafter;
for an undertaking performed contrary to the rules will result in the agitation of the Goddess and lead to one's downfall. 143.
Having understood everything from the scriptures, he realized that passion is a perilous obstacle;
my child, do not follow the path of the Yoginīs without the feet of the Guru. (144)
Even if the moon and the sun were to fall to the earth and shatter, even then this word of the Lord of the World would not become false. (145)
The Dharma, which is the man arisen from the secret [place] and the treasury of all accomplishments, was taught to me out of compassion by the Lord, the source of mercy. (146)
Just as a rutting elephant is brought under control by the wise through heavy nets and other means, so too is consciousness subdued by those of great realization. 147.
Just as a certain great medicine is both delicious and a destroyer of disease, so too does the bliss of wisdom and means effortlessly destroy the afflictions. (148)
To everyone, a beautiful woman is delightful; yet to those possessed by passion, she is for the pure-hearted a noose around the neck, while to others she is a knife that cuts their bonds. 149.
Oh, the power of the skillful means of those who follow the Mahāyāna! Embracing a passionate woman tightly, they enjoy the god of love himself. (150)

In this world, desire for sensual pleasures is a portion of disease that always yields only the fruit of manifold and dense passions; whereas those who delight in the essence of being are gladdened by the innate bliss of union.
Thus, with a mind repeatedly satisfied by the happiness of the world, one attains the reality (tathatā) of the entire universe without the exertion of afflictions. ||151||
Thus ends the *Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana*, titled "The Essence of All Yoginīs," as taught by the venerable Lokanātha in the *Guhyasamayatantra*, the *Mahāyoginījālatantra*.
This is the work of the accomplished master, Śabara-pāda.
